prompt: Amy, Bert, Carl, Doris and Ernst each rolled two dice and added the number of dots. Who rolled the largest total?

Peter is guessing Paul's password. Peter knows that Paul used only digits for the last three places and that it has at most three capital letters. Which of the following choices could be Paul's password?

solutions.title: Check both rules
solutions.body:
- PAUL123: 4 capital letters — too many.
- Pa1u2L3: ends in 2, L, 3 — L is not a digit.
- LUap4321: ends in 3, 2, 1 (digits) and has only 2 capitals (L, U). **Fits.**
- Paulin3: ends in i, n, 3 — not all digits.
- 123PAUL: ends in letters.

**Answer: (C) LUap4321**

solutions.title: Look at the ends first
solutions.body:
Only PAUL123 and LUap4321 end in three digits. PAUL123 has four capital letters, which is too many. So the password can only be LUap4321.

**Answer: (C) LUap4321**

prompt: George and his father go to the circus. Their seat numbers are 71 and 72. The sign shows where the seats are. Which way should they go?
Richard dries grapes to obtain raisins. He gets 1 kilogram of raisins out of 4 kilograms of grapes. How many kilograms of grapes will he need in order to obtain 4 kilograms of raisins?
What does Pipo see when he looks at himself in the mirror?
A rectangle is partly hidden behind a curtain. What is the shape of the hidden part?
Anna shared her apples among herself and five friends. If everyone got half an apple, how many apples did she share?

solutions.title: Count the people
solutions.body:
Anna and her 5 friends are 6 people. Each gets half an apple, and two halves make a whole apple, so 6 halves are $6 \div 2 = 3$ apples.

**Answer: (B) 3**

solutions.title: Pair up
solutions.body:
Put the 6 people into 3 pairs. Each pair shares one apple, so 3 apples were shared.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: Which tile fits in the middle such that lines of the same colour are joined together? (Turning the middle tile is allowed.)

solutions.title: Match the colours around the hole
solutions.body:
Go around the empty hexagon and write down which colour (red, blue or yellow) arrives at each of its six edges from the neighbouring tiles. The tile in the middle must have the same colour ending at each edge. Turning a tile only moves its pattern around; it does not change the order of the colours around the tile.

Going around the hole, the colours and their order match only tile (B): with the right turn, each of its red, blue and yellow line ends meets a line of the same colour.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Rule out by counting line ends
solutions.body:
Count how many red, blue and yellow lines end at the hole's edges, and which edges are joined together by the same line. A tile whose lines join the wrong pairs of edges (for example, two edges of different colours) cannot fit, however you turn it. This rules out (A), (C), (D) and (E).

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: The sum of the digits of the number 2016 is equal to 9: $2 + 0 + 1 + 6 = 9$. What is the next number that is greater than 2016 with the sum of its digits equal to 9?

The perimeter of the rectangle ABCD is 30 cm. Lisa cut off three rectangles as shown. She found that the sum of the three perimeters is equal to 20 cm. What is the perimeter of the figure obtained after the cutting?

solutions.title: Push the edges out
solutions.body:
All three cut-off rectangles sit in corners of ABCD. When you cut a rectangle out of a corner, the two sides you remove are replaced by two new sides of exactly the same lengths (just moved inwards). So the perimeter does not change.

Move every horizontal piece of the new boundary up or down and every vertical piece left or right: they fill the sides of ABCD exactly. The perimeter is still 30 cm. (The 20 cm is not needed.)

**Answer: (C) 30 cm**

solutions.title: Horizontal and vertical parts
solutions.body:
Look along any horizontal line: going from left to right along the top of the figure, the horizontal pieces together are exactly as long as AB, and the same along the bottom. Likewise the vertical pieces on the left and right add up to the height. So the perimeter is $2 \times (\text{length} + \text{width}) = 30$ cm, the same as ABCD.

**Answer: (C) 30 cm**

prompt: Five children had each a paper square, a paper triangle and a paper circle. Every child put their own papers in a pile, as shown in the pictures. How many children put the triangle after the square?
The mouse wants to escape from the maze. How many different paths can the mouse take without passing through the same opening more than once?

Zoe has two cards with numbers on both sides of the cards – four numbers in total. The sum of the four numbers equals 32; the sum of the two numbers on the first card is equal to the sum of the two numbers on the second card. What are the hidden numbers?

solutions.title: Half of 32
solutions.body:
The two cards have the same sum, and together they make 32, so each card adds up to $32 \div 2 = 16$.

- First card: $16 - 5 = 11$ on the back.
- Second card: $16 - 12 = 4$ on the back.

**Answer: (C) 11 and 4**

solutions.title: Check the choices
solutions.body:
The two hidden numbers must add up to $32 - 5 - 12 = 15$; this leaves (A), (C), (D) and (E). Only with 11 behind the 5 and 4 behind the 12 do both cards add up to the same number ($5 + 11 = 16 = 12 + 4$).

**Answer: (C) 11 and 4**

prompt: A farmer has the same number of chickens, sheep and goats. Together all these animals have 180 legs. How many goats live on this farm?

solutions.title: Make groups
solutions.body:
Put one chicken, one sheep and one goat in a group. A group has $2 + 4 + 4 = 10$ legs. $180 \div 10 = 18$ groups, so there are 18 goats.

**Answer: (C) 18**

Rachel added seven numbers together and got a sum of 2016. She later found out she had made a mistake by using the number 201 instead of 102. What sum should she have gotten instead of 2016?
Helena turns the card (shown at the top) over about its left-hand edge and then about its top edge, as shown. What does Helena see?

solutions.title: Two flips make a half-turn
solutions.body:
Turning the card over its left edge mirrors the picture left–right (and shows the plain back). Turning it over its top edge then mirrors it top–bottom and shows the front again. Both flips together are the same as turning the card halfway around (180°).

The card has a half circle in the bottom half with the black quarter on the left. After a half-turn the half circle is in the top half and the black quarter is on the right. That is picture (D).

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Follow the black quarter
solutions.body:
The black quarter starts at the bottom-left. After the flip over the left edge it is at the bottom-right; after the flip over the top edge it is at the top-right. Only (D) has the half circle on top with the black part at the top-right.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Tim, Tom and Jim are triplets (three brothers born on the same day). Their brother Paul is exactly 3 years older. Which of the following numbers could be the sum of the ages of the four brothers? (All ages are rounded to a whole year.)

A group of 31 students went camping taking nine tents. Each tent shelters either three or five students. If all students were covered by a tent, at least how many of the tents housed five students each?

solutions.title: Start with small tents
solutions.body:
If all 9 tents held 3 students, they would hold $9 \times 3 = 27$ students. We need $31 - 27 = 4$ more places. Each time a 3-tent is replaced by a 5-tent we gain 2 places, so we need $4 \div 2 = 2$ tents for five.

Check: $2 \times 5 + 7 \times 3 = 10 + 21 = 31$. ✓

**Answer: (A) 2**

solutions.title: Try the smallest choice
solutions.body:
With 2 big tents: $10$ students in them, and the other 7 tents hold $21$. Total 31 — it works, and 2 is the smallest choice.

**Answer: (A) 2**

prompt: The picture shows the roads between five connected towns. The numbers show the distances between the towns. It is 24 kilometres from Caramelshire to Nutyork. The distance between Vanillaton and Chocolateford is 10 km longer than the distance between Vanillaton and Candister. Nutyork is closer to Candister than it is to Chocolateford. How far is it from Candister to Chocolateford?

solutions.title: Place the towns
solutions.body:
Call the towns 1 to 5 from left to right; the roads are $1\text{–}2 = 23$, $2\text{–}3 = 13$, $3\text{–}4 = 11$, $4\text{–}5 = 35$.

- 24 km is only possible as $13 + 11$, so Caramelshire and Nutyork are towns 2 and 4, and town 3 lies between them.
- Vanillaton, Chocolateford and Candister are towns 1, 3 and 5. From town 3: to town 1 is $13 + 23 = 36$, to town 5 is $11 + 35 = 46$, and $46 - 36 = 10$. So Vanillaton is town 3, Chocolateford is town 5 and Candister is town 1.
- (Nutyork is town 2: 23 km from Candister, much closer than Chocolateford.)

Candister to Chocolateford is the whole road: $23 + 13 + 11 + 35 = 82$ km.

**Answer: (E) 82**

solutions.title: Ends of the road
solutions.body:
Once we know Vanillaton is in the middle (town 3) and the other two clue towns are at the ends, the distance between Candister and Chocolateford is the length of the whole road: $23 + 13 + 11 + 35 = 82$ km.

**Answer: (E) 82**
